lesson.title: Resistance in AC: power, moment by moment

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the dot on the power wave staying above the line and making two humps for every cycle of the voltage when you drag the time cursor along the in-step waves.
interactive.title: The power scrubber
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture, the power scrubber. The heater test's 10 Ω element, an example value, sits on an AC supply with a 100 V peak at 50 Hz. Above, its voltage wave and its current wave share one time axis, 0 to 40 ms, two cycles of 20 ms; the current wave is dashed, with its scale on the right, peaking at 100 ÷ 10 = 10 A. They cross zero and reach their tops together, because the current through a resistance is the voltage ÷ the resistance at every instant, so voltage × current is also voltage² ÷ 10, the heater test's humps, now built from two waves. Below, on the same time axis, is the power wave, voltage × current worked instant by instant. A time cursor, a vertical line through both graphs, is dragged from 0 to 40 ms and opens at 5 ms, the top of the first cycle. Where it crosses the waves, readouts give the voltage, the current and their product, and a dot lands on the power wave at that product: 100 V × 10 A = 1000 W at 5 ms. A flat dashed line marks the power wave's average, 500 W, labelled V_rms × I_rms. Screen 1 lets you drag the cursor and watch the dot ride the power wave. Screen 2 parks the cursor at 15 ms, the bottom of the cycle, with readouts of −100 V and −10 A, and asks for the power: 1000 W; −1000 W (the minus kept); or 0 W. A right Check drops the dot at 1000 W. Screen 3 sweeps the cursor along a whole cycle, leaving a trace: one hump from 0 to 1000 W while the voltage is forward and another while it is backward, each 10 ms long, so two humps for every cycle; a counter shows 100 humps a second on 50 Hz. Screen 4 asks how many humps a second a heater gives on the 60 Hz supply most common on board ship: 120; 60 (the supply's own frequency); or 240 (doubled twice). Screen 5 draws the dashed average at 500 W, half the 1000 W top, because the power is 100 sin × 10 sin = 1000 sin², 1000 W × the sine squared and a squared sine's humps fit exactly into its dips (Calculus fundamentals' fold). Beside it the rms values, 0.707 × 100 = 70.7 V and 0.707 × 10 = 7.07 A, multiply to about 500 W, because each is 1 ÷ √2 of its peak and 1 ÷ √2 squared is a half. Screen 6 shows the voltage and the current each averaging zero over a cycle and asks what the element averages: 500 W; 0 W (the averages multiplied); or 1000 W (the top of a hump). Screen 7 turns to the mains card: a 1 kW heater on 230 V mains, 230² ÷ 1000 = 52.9 Ω, drawing 230 ÷ 52.9 = 4.35 A rms. The voltage wave peaks at 325 V and the current at 4.35 × √2 = 6.15 A, so the dashed average sits at 230 × 4.35 = 1000 W and the humps reach twice that, 2000 W, about 325 × 6.15. Screen 8: a clamp meter reads 10 A on a heater at 230 V, and the meter and the 230 V are both rms; what is its average power, and how high do its humps reach? 2300 W with tops of 4600 W; 4600 W with tops of 9200 W (the peaks multiplied, about 325 V × 14.1 A, taken as the average); or 1150 W with tops of 2300 W (the rms product taken as the top). Screen 9, on the 10 Ω card, switches the supply to 60 Hz itself, then frees the switch, 50 Hz and 60 Hz, to flick back and forth: at 60 Hz the humps crowd closer, 120 a second, but their tops stay at 1000 W and the average at 500 W, because a resistor's current follows the voltage at each instant whatever the frequency. Screen 10: a heater's power humps top out at 3000 W; what is its average power? 1500 W; 3000 W (the top taken as the average); or 2120 W (0.707 used once on the power). Screens 11 and 12 are mixed. Screen 11: which is true of the 10 Ω element's power? It reaches zero twice each cycle and never goes below it; it goes below zero on the backward half; or it stays steady at 500 W. Screen 12: an example heater element across 440 V, the voltage most ships' systems run at, on the 60 Hz most common on board ship, draws 10 A; is its power 4.4 kW in 120 humps a second; 4.4 kW in 60 humps a second; or 8.8 kW in 120 humps a second (the peaks multiplied, about 622 V × 14.1 A, twice 4.4 kW)? Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. The closing line says the dot never goes below the line here because the voltage and current keep step, and that lessons 4 and 5 put in a coil and a capacitor, where it does.
interactive.ignores: The element is ideal: its resistance is held fixed, though a real element's resistance changes as it heats. The waves are pure sines; real mains is close to a sine rather than exactly one. Time is stretched so one 20 ms cycle fills half the screen. The 10 Ω element, the 100 V peak, the heaters and the meter readings are example values.

explain.text:
Feed a resistor AC and its power is not steady. Multiply the voltage by the current at each instant and you get a power wave that pulses twice for every cycle of the supply and never drops below zero, and for a resistance its average is the rms voltage times the rms current, just as volts times amps on DC.

In a resistor the current is the voltage ÷ the resistance at every instant, so the two waves rise and fall together: they reach their tops and bottoms at the same times.[^6] Waves that keep step like this are [[in phase]]. The power at any one instant is that instant's voltage times that instant's current, the P = V × I you use on DC, worked moment by moment: the [[instantaneous power]]. Take the heater test's 10 Ω element on a 100 V peak, so the current peaks at 10 A. At the top of the wave it takes 100 × 10 = 1000 W. As the wave crosses zero both are zero, so it takes nothing. On the backward half both are negative, −100 V and −10 A at the bottom, and a minus times a minus is a plus, so it takes 1000 W again: the element heats whichever way the current flows. So there is one hump of power on the forward half and another on the backward half. That is the heater test's row of humps again, now built from two waves: the current is the voltage ÷ 10 Ω at each instant, so voltage × current is voltage² ÷ 10. Multiplying the two waves is the form that lasts, because in later lessons the current will not keep step with the voltage. For a resistor the power wave never goes below zero,[^7] touching zero only as the waves cross it, and its frequency is double that of the voltage and current.[^8] On 50 Hz mains that is 100 humps a second.

The humps run from 0 to 1000 W. The power is 1000 W × the sine squared, and remember Calculus fundamentals' fold: a squared sine's humps fit exactly into its dips, so they average half their top, 500 W. That is the [[average power]], the heat the element actually gives. The rms values give it straight away. For a sine each is about 0.707 of its peak,[^2] so 70.7 V and 7.07 A, and 70.7 × 7.07 is about 500 W, because 0.707 is 1 ÷ √2 and 1 ÷ √2 squared is a half. For a resistance, the product of the rms voltage and the rms current equals the average power.[^9] The peaks multiplied give the top of each hump, twice the average, not the heat. Averaging first fails too: over a whole cycle the voltage and the current each average zero, yet the element still warms, because it is the product that has to be averaged, and here the product never goes below zero.

UK mains is 230 V nominal,[^3] peaking near 325 V.[^4] A 1 kW heater on it is 230² ÷ 1000 = 52.9 Ω and draws 230 ÷ 52.9 = 4.35 A, so its power averages 230 × 4.35 = 1000 W, in humps that reach twice that, 2000 W, 100 times a second. On the 60 Hz most common on board ship,[^1] the humps come 120 times a second. This is a simplified model, an ideal resistor on a pure sine; a real element's resistance changes as it warms, and real mains is close to a sine rather than exactly one. **In a resistor the voltage and current keep step, so the power wave never goes below zero,[^7] beats at twice the supply's frequency[^8] and averages the rms voltage times the rms current.[^9]**

analogy.text: A full-wave bridge rectifier on 50 Hz gives a row of humps all one way, 100 a second, because it turns the backward half of the wave forward. A resistor's power wave has the same look for a related reason: on the backward half the voltage and the current are both negative, and a minus times a minus is a plus, so the power is forward again.
analogy.breaks: The rectifier's diodes steer the backward half round, so its humps are the wave's size made positive, meet zero in sharp points and average 0.637 of the top. The resistor steers nothing: its current really does reverse every half cycle, and its power stays positive only because the voltage reverses with it. Its humps are a sine squared, touching zero smoothly, so they average half the top.

practice.text:
- Take the rms voltage and the rms current. Appliances and devices are commonly quoted in rms values, rather than peak values.[^10]
- For a heater, an element or any plain resistance, multiply them: average power = V_rms × I_rms.[^9]
- The power humps top out at twice that, for a sine, and come at twice the supply's frequency.[^8]
- For a motor, or anything with a coil or a capacitor, V × I is not yet the watts; lessons 4, 5 and 8 show why.

**Rule of thumb:** On a resistance, watts = rms volts × rms amps, and the hump tops are twice that, 100 a second on 50 Hz.

**Worked example:** A clamp meter reads 10 A on a heater at 230 V. Its power is 230 × 10 = 2300 W. Its voltage peaks at 325 V and its current at 14.1 A, so the humps top out at twice 2300 W, 4600 W, for an instant each, about 325 × 14.1.

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying the peaks, about 325 × 14.1 = 4600 W. That is the top of each hump, twice the heat.
- Averaging first. The voltage and current each average zero over a cycle; the power does not.
- Expecting the power to go below zero on the backward half. In a resistor both are negative together, so the power stays positive.[^7]
- Expecting the power to pulse at the supply's frequency. It pulses at twice it.[^8]
- Using V × I as the watts of a motor. It works on a resistance; a coil changes it.

sources.quote: Misconception: Peak voltage is the same as mains voltage. Correction: UK mains voltage is 230 V RMS, so the peak voltage is about 325 V (230 × √2).

sources.title: maritime electrical installations - notes on design ...
sources.quote: The majority of ships have a 3 phase, 3 wire, 440V insulated neutral system. This means that the neutral point of star connected generators is not earthed to the ship's hull. For Continental European vessels, a 380V, 3 phase system is common.

sources.title: Lessons In Electric Circuits -- Volume II (AC) - Chapter 11
sources.quote: Note that the waveform for power is always positive, never negative for this resistive circuit. This means that power is always being dissipated by the resistive load, and never returned to the source as it is with reactive loads.

sources.title: Lessons In Electric Circuits -- Volume II (AC) - Chapter 11
sources.quote: Also note that the waveform for power is not at the same frequency as the voltage or current! Rather, its frequency is double that of either the voltage or current waveforms.

interactive.html:
Voltage and current above, power below.

Elements, peaks and meter readings are example values; the power at each instant is the voltage × the current.
interactive.title: The power scrubber
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the dot on the power wave staying above the line and making two humps for every cycle of the voltage when you drag the time cursor along the in-step waves.

checks.label: Both curves reach their maxima and minima at the same times, that is, the current through and the voltage across the resistor are in phase: on every card the drawn current is the drawn voltage ÷ the resistance at each instant, and its tops and bottoms fall at the voltage's

The waveform for power is always positive, never negative for this resistive circuit: on every screen each drawn point of the power wave is the drawn voltage × the drawn current at that instant, and none is below zero

The waveform for power is not at the same frequency as the voltage or current; its frequency is double that of either: the drawn power wave has a hump at every top and every bottom of the voltage, two a cycle, shown as 100 humps a second on 50 Hz and 120 on 60 Hz

The product of the RMS voltage and RMS current is equal to the average power: on the 10 Ω, mains, clamp-meter and ship cards the dashed average sits at the mean of the drawn power wave over whole humps, and the row under it multiplies the rms values to that figure: 500 W, 1000 W, 2300 W and 4.4 kW
For a sine wave, the RMS value is approximately 0.707 of its peak value: on the 10 Ω card the rows read Vrms = 0.707 × 100 V = 70.7 V and Irms = 0.707 × 10 A = 7.07 A
UK mains voltage is 230 V RMS, so the peak voltage is about 325 V (230 × √2): on the mains card the voltage wave reaches 325 V at the top of each cycle and −325 V at the bottom
UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: the 1 kW mains heater is 230² ÷ 1000 = 52.9 Ω and draws 230 ÷ 52.9 = 4.35 A, its power humps reaching 2000 W and averaging 1000 W
60 Hz is the most common frequency adopted for use on board ship: the ship screens run at 60 Hz, and once answered show 2 humps a cycle × 60 Hz = 120 humps a second
The majority of ships have a 3 phase, 3 wire, 440V insulated neutral system: the ship heater runs at 440 V rms, its wave peaking at 440 × √2 = 622 V, and drawing 10 A it averages 440 × 10 = 4.4 kW
The scrubber multiplies: at 5 ms 100 V × 10 A = 1000 W; at 10 ms both are 0, so the power is 0; at 15 ms −100 V × −10 A = +1000 W
The fold: the top of a hump above the 500 W average, moved on half a hump (5 ms) and turned over, lies exactly along the dip beside it

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer; before an answer its picture hides what is asked (the power there, the power wave, the average or the humps a second), and each wrong pick draws what it claims, in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: Screen 7 says 4.35 × 1.41 = 6.15 A, but 4.35 × 1.41 is 6.13; 6.15 A comes from multiplying by √2 itself (1.414), so the shown sum is wrong as written.

The worked example says 230² ÷ 2300 = 23 Ω "checks it as a resistance", but working out a resistance from the same readings cannot show the load is resistive, and 23 Ω is not one of the lesson’s listed numbers.
